result: Seven chimpanzee iPSC lines were generated from healthy donors (4 female, 3 male, ages 9-17) using episomal plasmids expressing OCT3/4, SOX2, KLF4, L-MYC, LIN28, shRNA targeting TP53, and EBNA1 mRNA. Fibroblasts from 5 individuals were purchased from Coriell Institute, while 2 (C6, C7) were derived from skin biopsies at Yerkes Primate Research Center. All lines are available to other investigators upon request.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 and C163-C164 provide comprehensive documentation of the generation of 7 chimpanzee iPSC lines, including donor demographics, source materials, reprogramming methodology, and availability. The episomal approach is well-documented in cited literature (Okita et al., 2011; Howden et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2011), and the methodology is described in sufficient detail for reproducibility.

result: Chimpanzee iPSC lines closely resemble human iPSCs in morphology, can be maintained for at least 60 passages without loss of pluripotency or self-renewal on both MEF feeder cells and feeder-free conditions, and exhibit normal karyotypes after reprogramming and >15 passages.
evaluation: Claims C6-C8 and C165-C166 are supported by visual evidence (Figure 1A-B) and explicit statements about culture stability and karyotype analysis. The 60-passage threshold and normal karyotypes after >15 passages provide strong evidence for genomic stability, which is critical for iPSC characterization.

result: All chimpanzee iPSC lines express pluripotency markers (OCT3/4, SOX2, NANOG, Tra-1-81, SSEA4) and show endogenous expression of pluripotency genes with no exogenous gene expression after 10 passages or genomic integration/episomal retention after 15 passages, indicating self-renewal is maintained solely through endogenous gene expression.
evaluation: Claims C9-C15 are supported by immunocytochemistry (Figure 1C, supplements), qPCR (Figure 1D), and PCR analysis (Figure 1E). The absence of exogenous gene expression and episomal retention after extended passaging provides strong evidence that pluripotency is maintained endogenously, which is a critical validation for episomal reprogramming.

result: All 7 chimpanzee iPSC lines demonstrate pluripotency through spontaneous differentiation into three germ layers in embryoid body assays, directed differentiation to hepatocytes and cardiomyocytes, and teratoma formation in immunodeficient mice containing tissues from all three germ layers, with chimpanzee origin confirmed by mitochondrial DNA sequencing.
evaluation: Claims C16-C21 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including immunocytochemistry (Figure 2A), directed differentiation protocols (Figure 2 supplement 2, Video 1), histological analysis of teratomas (Figure 2B, supplement 3), and Sanger sequencing of mitochondrial DNA (Figure 2 supplement 4). The combination of in vitro and in vivo differentiation assays provides comprehensive validation of pluripotency.

result: All chimpanzee iPSC lines have PluriTest pluripotency scores >20 but novelty scores >1.67 (which in human PSCs suggests chromosomal abnormalities or differentiation). However, unlike human PSCs with high novelty scores, chimpanzee lines are easily maintained and differentiate into all three germ layers, suggesting high novelty scores reflect inter-species regulatory differences rather than abnormalities.
evaluation: Claims C22-C27 are supported by PluriTest analysis (Figure 3A-B) and functional validation from embryoid body and teratoma assays (C16-C21). The interpretation that high novelty scores reflect inter-species differences rather than defects is reasonable given the demonstrated pluripotency and differentiation capacity. However, this interpretation is speculative (C27) and would benefit from additional validation.

result: Genome-wide RNA-seq and DNA methylation data were generated from all 7 chimpanzee iPSC lines (derived from fibroblasts) and 7 human iPSC lines (derived from fibroblasts and LCLs from Caucasian and Yoruba individuals). Gene expression analysis was restricted to 12,171 orthologous genes, and DNA methylation to 335,307 conserved probes to prevent biases from genetic divergence.
evaluation: Claims C28-C34 describe the experimental design and data generation approach. The restriction to orthologous genes and conserved probes is methodologically sound for inter-species comparisons (citing Blekhman et al., 2010; Hernando-Herraez et al., 2013). The study design intentionally includes different cell types of origin for human iPSCs to demonstrate that regulatory differences are not due to technical factors (C31).

result: PCA shows clear separation of human and chimpanzee iPSCs along PC1 (p<10^-13 for expression, p<10^-12 for methylation), with human PC2 driven by ethnicity. At 1% FDR, 4609 genes (37.9%) are differentially expressed between species, mostly with small fold-changes. No GO BP terms are enriched at 5% FDR for all DE genes, but 123 terms are enriched for 546 genes with |log2FC|>2. High concordance (72.2%, 98.24% directional) with Marchetto et al. (2013b).
evaluation: Claims C35-C42 are supported by PCA (Figure 4A-B), differential expression analysis, and comparison with prior work. The statistical significance is strong (p<10^-13), and the concordance with Marchetto et al. validates the findings. The lack of GO enrichment for all DE genes but enrichment for high-FC genes (C39-C40) is appropriately reported and suggests most differences are subtle.

result: 63,791 probes are differentially methylated (DM) between species at 1% FDR, with 26,554 having mean β difference ≥0.1. These group into 3,529 DMRs, of which 2,348 associate with single genes. Of 1,350 expressed genes with DMRs, 558 (41.3%) are DE (p=0.1). DMRs are enriched for GO terms related to neurogenesis and skeletal development, but DE genes with DMRs show no GO enrichment.
evaluation: Claims C43-C52 describe DNA methylation differences with appropriate statistical thresholds and effect sizes. The association between DMRs and DE genes is modest (41.3%, p=0.1), suggesting methylation differences don't strongly predict expression changes. The enrichment of DMRs in developmental processes (C49-C51) is interesting but the lack of enrichment for DE genes with DMRs (C52) suggests complex regulatory relationships.

result: ChIP-seq analysis of H3K27me3 and H3K27ac in 3 chimpanzee iPSCs compared to 3 human iPSCs from Roadmap Epigenomics shows high overlap in H3K27me3 (90.1% of 2,604 bivalent genes enriched in both species, p<10^-16) and H3K27ac (95.8% of human genes enriched in chimpanzees). However, chimpanzees show excess H3K27ac signal. Of 22 pluripotency factors, 15 show H3K27ac in both species, with REX1 and ZFX enriched only in humans.
evaluation: Claims C53-C63 are supported by ChIP-seq analysis (Figure 5) with appropriate statistical significance (p<10^-16). The high overlap in histone modifications supports conserved pluripotency mechanisms. However, the excess H3K27ac in chimpanzees (C58) may reflect technical batch effects (acknowledged by authors), and the species-specific enrichment of REX1 and ZFX (C63) warrants further investigation. The comparison to public data introduces potential batch effects that could confound interpretation.

result: Of 16 core pluripotency transcription factors with expression data, 4 (E2F1, ESRRB, SALL4, REX1) are DE at 1% FDR, with ESRRB and REX1 showing |log2FC|>1. REX1 is expressed at low/undetectable levels in 6/7 chimpanzee iPSCs (mean RPKM=0.667) but high in all human iPSCs (mean RPKM=180.58) and one chimpanzee line (C6). REX1 promoter is highly methylated in 6 chimpanzee lines (mean β=0.87) but shows low methylation in humans and C6. No H3K27ac peaks at REX1 TSS in 3 chimpanzee lines (not including C6).
evaluation: Claims C64-C73 are supported by RNA-seq (Figure 6A), DNA methylation (Figure 6B), and ChIP-seq data (Figure 5D). The dramatic difference in REX1 expression between species (>250-fold) with corresponding methylation and histone modification differences provides strong multi-omic evidence. The exception of C6 expressing REX1 is important for interpreting functional consequences.

result: REX1 encodes a transcription factor present in all placental mammals and is established as a pluripotency marker in human and mouse PSCs. Multiple publications suggest REX1 maintains pluripotency and inhibits differentiation, but REX1-knockout mouse ESCs can form chimeric animals and homozygous null mice are viable, suggesting REX1 may not be indispensable for murine pluripotency. In humans, REX1 knockdown is associated with rapid loss of pluripotency, decreased glycolytic activity, and lack of mature mesodermal structures in teratomas.
evaluation: Claims C74-C82 accurately summarize prior literature on REX1 function, citing appropriate sources (Brivanlou et al., 2003; Masui et al., 2008; Scotland et al., 2009; Son et al., 2013). The apparent contradiction between mouse and human REX1 requirements (C77-C82) is correctly noted and provides important context for interpreting the chimpanzee findings.

result: Among genes downstream of REX1, only glycolysis genes show enrichment for DE (19/34 genes, p<0.01), but the direction contradicts prior reports—genes downregulated by REX1 knockdown (PGAM1, LDHA) have higher expression in chimpanzee iPSCs. REX1-expressing line C6 is not an outlier for glycolysis gene expression, suggesting inter-species differences are not due to REX1 expression. Teratomas and EBs from REX1-negative chimpanzee iPSCs show all three germ layers. REX1 is absent/low in bonobo iPSCs but expressed in chimpanzee iPSCs from Marchetto et al., suggesting variable REX1 loss doesn't impair pluripotency and its functions may be fulfilled by other mechanisms in chimpanzees.
evaluation: Claims C83-C91 present intriguing findings but the interpretation is uncertain. The opposite direction of glycolysis gene expression (C84) compared to Son et al. (2013) is puzzling and unexplained. The lack of outlier status for C6 (C85-C86) and normal differentiation of REX1-negative lines (C87) suggest REX1 is dispensable in chimpanzees, but this contradicts human data. The comparison to Marchetto et al. data (C88-C89) provides some support but is limited. The conclusion that other mechanisms compensate (C91) is speculative without identifying those mechanisms. Additional functional validation (e.g., REX1 overexpression in chimpanzee iPSCs or knockdown in C6) would strengthen these claims.

result: RNA-seq and DNA methylation data were collected from all iPSC precursor cell lines, yielding RPKM values for 13,147 genes across 28 samples. PCA shows PC1 is significantly associated with tissue type (p<10^-27 for expression, p<10^-17 for methylation) while PC2 separates species (p=0.001 for expression, p<10^-4 for methylation). Chimpanzee iPSCs have significantly higher DNA methylation than their precursor fibroblasts (p<10^-15), consistent with prior observations in human PSCs. iPSCs are remarkably homogeneous within species compared to precursors (p<10^-14 for methylation, p<10^-9 for expression) with reduced coefficients of variation (p<10^-6).
evaluation: Claims C92-C100 are supported by PCA (Figure 7), statistical comparisons, and citations to prior work (Bock et al., 2011; Nazor et al., 2012). The finding that iPSCs are more homogeneous than precursors (C99-C100) is important and well-supported statistically. The increased methylation in iPSCs (C97) is consistent with prior literature (C98), providing validation.

result: Within-species comparisons identify 9,235 DE genes between chimpanzee fibroblasts and iPSCs, and 7,765 (all precursors), 8,087 (LCL-derived), or 5,489 (fibroblast-derived) DE genes in humans. Similarly, 18,029 DMRs between chimpanzee fibroblasts and iPSCs, and 12,078 DMRs between human precursors and iPSCs. No GO categories are significantly overrepresented in any DE gene sets.
evaluation: Claims C101-C107 describe within-species reprogramming changes with appropriate statistical analysis (1% FDR). The large numbers of DE genes and DMRs are expected for reprogramming. The lack of GO enrichment (C107) is notable but may reflect the broad nature of reprogramming changes affecting many pathways.

result: Inter-species comparisons of precursors identify 5,663 DE genes, 84,747 DM probes, and 9,107 DMRs between chimpanzee fibroblasts and human precursors (LCLs+fibroblasts), but most differences reflect cell type variation (6,324 DE genes and 70,312 DM probes between human fibroblasts and LCLs). Comparing only fibroblasts identifies 1,236 DE genes and 25,456 DM probes between species, and 1,118 DE genes and 16,392 DM probes between corresponding iPSCs. No GO enrichment in any gene sets.
evaluation: Claims C108-C118 appropriately account for cell type differences (C111-C113) before making inter-species comparisons. The analysis restricted to fibroblasts (C114-C117) is more appropriate for inter-species comparison and shows reduced power due to smaller sample size (only 2 human fibroblast-derived iPSCs). The lack of GO enrichment (C118) is consistent with C107.

result: The overlap of inter-species DE genes (13.6%) and DM probes (11.8%) between iPSCs and precursors is considerable, but a large number of regulatory differences are observed only between iPSC lines. This observation is robust to different normalization approaches, strongly suggesting many differences between chimpanzee and human iPSC lines are intrinsic features of the pluripotent state in these species.
evaluation: Claims C119-C122 are supported by overlap analysis (Figure 7 supplement 3) and robustness testing (Figure 7 supplement 4). The finding that many regulatory differences are iPSC-specific (C121) rather than inherited from precursors is important and suggests species-specific pluripotency mechanisms. The robustness to different normalization approaches (C122) strengthens this conclusion.

result: Retroviral vector silencing in chimpanzee iPSCs was not as stable as in human iPSCs generated using the same method. The use of episomal vectors circumvents problems of random exogenous gene reactivation and disruption of the host genome through retroviral integration.
evaluation: Claims C127-C128 are supported by data (Figure 1 supplement 5) and citation (Sommer et al., 2012). The observation of unstable retroviral silencing in chimpanzees (C127) provides important justification for the episomal approach and highlights a potential species-specific difference in reprogramming. This is a valuable methodological contribution.

result: The panel of seven chimpanzee iPSC lines is powerful enough to robustly detect inter-species differences in gene expression, splicing and regulation. The panel contains both female and male lines, allowing for future studies of sex-specific differences in gene expression.
evaluation: Claims C129-C130 are reasonable inferences based on the successful detection of thousands of DE genes and DMRs. The inclusion of both sexes (4 female, 3 male from C2) enables sex-specific analyses, as demonstrated by XIST expression analysis (Figure 7 supplement 6). The sample size (n=7) is adequate for the analyses performed.

result: At transcriptional and epigenetic levels, iPSCs are remarkably homogeneous within and between species, more so than precursors, aligning with understanding of pluripotency as a complex, highly regulated state. Strong H3K27me3 overlap supports this. However, over 4,500 DE genes and 3,500 DMRs exist between species—more than in other tissues with similar sample sizes—likely due to increased power from low intra-species variability enabling detection of small differences (supported by higher fraction of genes with log2FC<2 detected as DE).
evaluation: Claims C131-C138 synthesize major findings with appropriate interpretation. The homogeneity of iPSCs (C131, C133) is well-supported by data (C99-C100, C56). The large number of inter-species differences (C134-C136) is explained by increased statistical power (C137-C138), which is a reasonable interpretation supported by Figure 4 supplement 2. The comparison to prior work (C136) provides context.

result: A subset of small magnitude regulatory differences between human and chimpanzee iPSCs may be biologically relevant, as inter-species regulatory differences in methylation levels are enriched in regions associated with developmental processes.
evaluation: Claims C139-C140 are supported by GO enrichment analysis (Supplementary files 4-5) showing DMRs enriched for developmental processes (C49-C51). While C139 is speculative about biological relevance, the enrichment in developmental genes (C140) provides some support. However, the lack of functional validation limits confidence in biological relevance.

result: iPSCs have potential to transform understanding of non-model organism biology and facilitate functional comparative studies. The chimpanzee iPSC lines meet all pluripotency criteria and provide an avenue for investigating how gene expression/regulation changes underlie phenotypic differences. Through directed differentiation, functional studies could be performed in cell types with a priori hypotheses about selective pressure. This enables testing the hypothesis that developmental gene regulation changes underlie phenotypic differences between primates and provides insights into human-specific adaptations.
evaluation: Claims C123-C126, C141-C145, C156, C161-C162 describe the potential applications and significance of the work. The pluripotency validation (C124) is well-supported by C16-C21. The potential for comparative developmental studies (C125-C126, C143-C144) is reasonable given the demonstrated pluripotency and differentiation capacity, though optimization of protocols will be needed (C142). These claims appropriately describe future directions and significance rather than making unsupported assertions about current findings.

result: Much less within-species variation is observed in iPSCs than in somatic cells, indicating reprogramming erases many inter-individual differences. The low within-species regulatory variation in iPSCs allowed identification of many novel inter-species regulatory differences of small magnitude.
evaluation: Claims C146-C147 summarize key findings supported by C99-C100 (homogeneity data) and C137-C138 (power to detect small differences). This is an important conclusion that explains how the study design enabled detection of subtle inter-species differences that might be missed in more variable tissues.

result: Comparative primate studies have been hindered by limited sample availability, ethical concerns constraining work to LCLs and fibroblasts, and reliance on post-mortem materials or model organisms with assumptions of functional conservation. Reprogramming to iPSCs has become routine for human and mouse but not widespread in non-human primates. The broadest iPSC application has been patient-derived lines for disease modeling, which display relevant phenotypes in vitro.
evaluation: Claims C148-C160 accurately describe the state of the field with appropriate citations (Gallego Romero et al., 2012; Blekhman et al., 2008, 2010; Brawand et al., 2011; Enard et al., 2009; Cotney et al., 2013; Prabhakar et al., 2008; McLean et al., 2011; Rockman et al., 2005; Pollard et al., 2006; Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006; Takahashi et al., 2007; Ezashi et al., 2009; Ben-Nun et al., 2011; Nagy et al., 2011; Marchetto et al., 2013b; Cohen and Melton, 2011; Israel et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012; Merkle and Eggan, 2013; Wang et al., 2014). This provides appropriate context for the significance of the work.
